source.author: stat
source.text: stant tristes horrore comae, vittasque prementes caesaries insana levat: diducta putares lumina consumptumque genis rediisse nitorem.
source.text_original: stant tristes horrore comae, vittasque prementes / caesaries insana levat: diducta putares / lumina consumptumque genis rediisse nitorem.
source.text_english: Their hair stands on end in horror; their mad mane, pressing down their headbands, lifts itself up: you would think their eyes were drawn apart, and that the brightness had returned to their cheeks, though spent.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Minyas ambage ducemque terrificat; sed enim contra Phoebeius Idmon, non pallore viris, non ullo horrore comarum terribilis, plenus fatis Phoeboque quieto, cui genitor tribuit monitu praenoscere divum omina, seu flammas seu lubrica comminus exta seu plenum certis interroget aera pennis, sic sociis Mopsoque canit:
reuse.text_original: Minyas ambage ducemque / terrificat; sed enim contra Phoebeius Idmon, / non pallore viris, non ullo horrore comarum / terribilis, plenus fatis Phoeboque quieto, / cui genitor tribuit monitu praenoscere divum / omina, seu flammas seu lubrica comminus exta / seu plenum certis interroget aera pennis, / sic sociis Mopsoque canit:
reuse.text_english: He terrifies the Minyae with a roundabout tale and their leader; but on the other side Phoebus’ Idmon, not dreadful to men with paleness, not with any horrid mane of hair, but full of fate and of a calm Phoebus, to whom his father granted by his warning to know in advance the omens of the gods, whether he asks the flames, or slippery entrails at close range, or the air full of assured wings, thus sings to his companions and to Mopsus:
